VERDICT: EXTEND C0004 | FIND: `scan_health()` can also falsely mark a tool as available when the binary exists but execution times out. Evidence: `_run_tool()` returns `CompletedProcess(..., returncode=-1, stderr="TIMEOUT")` on timeout; each runner only special-cases `"NOT_FOUND"` and otherwise returns `[]`; `scan_health()` sets `tools_available[tool_name] = True` whenever the runner returns normally. FOLLOW: This is not just a parsing-loss issue. On timeout, the health scan reports the tool as healthy/available while silently dropping all diagnostics, so the insect brain receives a misleading “0 findings from available tool” signal and human reviewers cannot distinguish “clean” from “tool stalled”. FIX: same root fix as C0004/C0001 — propagate execution status from `_run_tool`/runner into `scan_health()` and mark timed-out tools unavailable or failed, not available.

FINDING_ID: F001
SEVERITY: 0.95
FLAW_CLASS: 2
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.71
DESCRIPTION: FIND — `evaluate_fix()` does not sandbox imports or project context, so fix evaluation is not actually testing the patched program in isolation. Evidence: it copies only the target file to `tmpdir` as `patched_path = os.path.join(tmpdir, os.path.basename(target_path))`, then runs `run_pyright/run_ruff/run_bandit` on that lone file. For tests, it runs `test_cmd` with `cwd=tmpdir`, but does not copy the rest of the repo, package structure, sibling modules, configs, or tests into the sandbox. Any fix touching imports or cross-file interfaces is therefore evaluated against a non-representative environment. The module docstring explicitly promises “sandboxed (tempdir, never modifies actual source)” and asks whether fix evaluation “actually sandbox correctly”; this implementation isolates writes, but not project semantics.
FOLLOW: Downstream, the immune pipeline’s Stage 4 uses `evaluate_fixes()` to mark findings `verified=True` when verdict is SAFE or NEUTRAL. That verified flag feeds NK “bug closed” logic in later rounds. Because evaluation is done on a single detached file, cross-module breakage can be missed and fixes can be incorrectly marked SAFE/NEUTRAL, causing the system to close bugs prematurely and suppress further review of still-broken findings. Conversely, valid fixes can be mislabeled harmful because imports/config expected from repo root are absent in `tmpdir`, preventing end-to-end trustworthy fix verification — a core advertised endocrine feature.
PROPOSED_FIX: FIX — when evaluating a fix, copy the full relevant source tree rooted at the common parent of `source_paths` into the temp directory, preserve relative paths, apply the patch to the copied target file there, and run tool/test commands against that copied tree instead of a single basename-only file.
VERIFIED: TRUE

FINDING_ID: F002
SEVERITY: 0.91
FLAW_CLASS: 5
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.63
DESCRIPTION: FIND — `evaluate_fix()` can silently classify a fix as SAFE/NEUTRAL when analysis tools did not run at all on the patched file. Evidence: baseline and post-fix counts come from `_count_tool_issues()`, which returns `0` on any exception. The tool runners themselves return `[]` for `"NOT_FOUND"` and currently also for timeout paths unless separately handled. `_compute_fix_verdict()` then treats `total_net == 0` plus `tests_passed is True` as SAFE, or `tests_passed is None` as NEUTRAL. There is no field recording whether pyright/ruff/bandit actually executed successfully before using their counts in the verdict.
FOLLOW: This directly affects the immune pipeline’s programmatic verification step. A finding with a proposed fix can be marked `verified=True` even when static analysis never executed, because zero-before/zero-after is interpreted as no regression. That false verification propagates into later rounds through the canonical finding flags, triggering NK duplicate closure and preventing models from revisiting a bug. This is silently wrong output, not mere observability loss.
PROPOSED_FIX: FIX — track per-tool execution success in `FixEvaluation` and make `_compute_fix_verdict()` return `UNEVALUABLE` unless the required before/after tool runs completed successfully (or were explicitly disabled), rather than treating missing data as zero issues.
VERIFIED: TRUE

FINDING_ID: F003
SEVERITY: 0.84
FLAW_CLASS: 2
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.58
DESCRIPTION: FIND — test execution in `evaluate_fix()` can run against the real repository instead of the patched sandbox, so the “tests_passed” signal is not tied to the applied fix. Evidence: the function invokes `_run_tool(test_cmd, cwd=tmpdir)`, but does not rewrite path arguments inside `test_cmd`, set `PYTHONPATH`, or ensure the command references files inside the copied sandbox. In current immune pipeline usage, the command is `["python3", "-m", "pytest", "bench/tests/", ...]`; from `cwd=tmpdir`, that relative path usually does not exist in the sandbox because only one file was copied there. If the command uses absolute paths or Python imports resolve from elsewhere, tests can exercise the live repo rather than the patched candidate. Either way, the result is detached from the patched artifact under evaluation.
FOLLOW: A passed test suite can be reported for a fix that was never actually exercised, inflating SAFE verdicts; or tests can fail spuriously because expected repo paths are absent, inflating HARMFUL verdicts. Since `tests_passed=False` forces `HARMFUL`, and `tests_passed=True` can force `SAFE` even with no diagnostic improvement, this misbinding materially corrupts fix evaluation outcomes and the verified-fix closure path downstream.
PROPOSED_FIX: FIX — execute tests only against the copied project tree in the sandbox by rewriting/constructing the test command relative to that copied root (or using absolute paths within tmpdir), and if that cannot be guaranteed, set `tests_passed=None` and return `UNEVALUABLE` instead of trusting the result.
VERIFIED: TRUE

FINDING_ID: F004
SEVERITY: 0.72
FLAW_CLASS: 5
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.41
DESCRIPTION: FIND — `_find_target_file()` can select the wrong source file by substring match. Evidence: it returns a path if `sp_path.endswith(match) or match in sp_path`. The `match in sp_path` branch is overly loose: a mention like `brain.py` can match `insect_brain.py`; directory fragments can also collide across unrelated paths. The function then falls back to the first source path if no precise match exists.
FOLLOW: Fix evaluation can patch and analyze the wrong file while still producing a concrete verdict. Because the result is keyed only by `finding_id`, downstream consumers will believe the proposed fix was evaluated for the intended bug. This can produce both false SAFE and false HARMFUL classifications and undermine verified-fix propagation.
PROPOSED_FIX: FIX — remove the generic substring match and resolve only by exact normalized path match, basename match, or suffix path-component match; if resolution is ambiguous, return `None` and mark the fix `UNEVALUABLE` instead of guessing.
VERIFIED: TRUE

FINDING_ID: F005
SEVERITY: 0.68
FLAW_CLASS: 5
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.44
DESCRIPTION: FIND — `_apply_fix_to_source()` can apply a “whole-file replacement” for any syntactically valid 5+ line Python snippet, even when the snippet is only an explanatory excerpt and not a full file. Evidence: after `compile(fix, "<fix>", "exec")`, it unconditionally returns `fix` if `fix.count("\n") >= 5`; there is no check that the content resembles the original module, preserves imports, or was intended as a full replacement. Many review fixes are multi-line code fragments.
FOLLOW: The evaluator can replace the entire module with a partial snippet, then run tools on that artificial file and report a verdict about the proposed fix. This distorts the SAFE/HARMFUL signal and can incorrectly reject otherwise valid fixes or accept malformed ones. Since fix evaluation is used to close bugs programmatically, the misapplied patch mechanism undermines the feature’s core purpose.
PROPOSED_FIX: FIX — only treat `proposed_fix` as a whole-file replacement when it is explicitly marked as full-file content (for example by requiring it to start with the original module header/path marker or another clear full-file indicator); otherwise, if no search/replace or line-level rule matches, return `None`.
VERIFIED: TRUE
